Question: Can matter undergo continuous phase transitions?
Old_Answer: Generally matter is always phase transitioning in both directions, at any temperature. For example, water even at room temperature will have molecules leaving the liquid state and joining the gaseous state, and other molecules leaving the gaseous state and joining the liquid state. It’s a matter of the rates. At room temperature, it’s much more likely for a molecule to transition from gas to liquid than from liquid to gas, so you wind up with “most” of your molecules in liquid form. There is always a partial pressure of water vapor present as well though. As you raise the temperature, you raise the chance of a liquid-to-gas transition and lower the chance of a gas-to-liqud transition, so the proportion of water in the liquid and gas states will adjust. At exactly the boiling point, the probability of a molecule transitioning is the same in either direction. So, these things are always happening. Stay safe and well! Old_Answer: Well, Earth is constantly attracting the object via gravity. So, if you counteract any portion of that force, then… you are exerting some force on the object. Near Earth’s surface the gravitational force is generally regarded as producing a constant acceleration g on the object, directed toward the center of the earth (which we call “down”). So, neglecting air resistance, if the object is not accelerating at g toward the center of Earth, then you must be exerting a force on it. Of course, we’re talking about the vertical direction here - you could exert a force in some other direction. Under normal conditions, the up/down acceleration of gravity is g downward, and the sideways acceleration of gravity is zero. You can apply the same reasoning as above horizontally too - unless the object’s acceleration is g downward and zero sideways, you’re doing something. Stay safe and well! Question: What is the quantum field theory for someone just starting to learn it?
Old_Answer: It’s a lot of math that’s fairly hard to learn, for one thing. Conceptually it’s not that awful - the basic process you go through is that you know what your “initial conditions” are (the particles you have coming in toward a potential interaction). You then basically guess at possible final configurations (particles created, annihilated, etc., and how they are behaving), and then you can calculate the probability of the initial config leading to that final config. You repeat this process for more guessed final configs, until the total probability you have accounted for so far gets close enough to 1.0 to suit you. If it’s well below 1.0, then there’s some final configuration you haven’t considered yet. That’s basically it. The math takes care of enforcing conservation laws and all other physical requirements. The big difference between this and classical physics is that you do not “calculate” the final configuration - you “propose it” (guess at it) and then see how likely that is.
